Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

new paragraph for now the pond looks calm and the fish are eating but i will keep an eye on the water level because the warm spell has lasted longer than i expected the mark on the flat rock is about an inch below the waterline from last week and that could be evaporation i haven't topped it up yet the garden hose was left in the sun yesterday so i will run it briefly away from the pond before using it i would rather add a little water slowly than fill the pond in one go and stir up the bottom i should also put the test strips back in their sealed pouch the box sat open on the bench while i was writing the readings that's all for this memo", "output": "I wanted to leave a voice memo about the pond before I forget what I did this weekend. The water is still clear enough to see the pale stones on the bottom, but there is a green film starting on the inside of the shallow shelf. I used the soft brush and worked from the steps toward the pump intake so I wouldn't sweep loose leaves into it. The brush lifted some of the film, but not all of it, and I stopped rather than scrub the liner. The pond is roughly nine feet across at the widest point, and the shelf is about twelve inches deep. The deeper middle is closer to thirty inches, and the heron has been standing by the fence again. I moved the little wire cover back over the plants after I finished because it had slipped when I reached for the brush.

The pump was making a faint rattling sound on Saturday morning when I first switched it on. I shut it off and checked the basket for twigs. There was one small maple stem and a piece of string in there. The string was probably from the plant tie I cut last month. I rinsed the basket with pond water from a bucket instead of tap water and put it back in place. The rattle stopped, but I could still hear a low hum near the outlet. I checked that the hose had not kinked behind the flat rock, and the flow looked steady. I haven't opened the pump housing because the manual says to disconnect power and wait until the unit is cool before removing the cover. I need to find the narrow screwdriver that fits those screws before I do that.

I tested the water with the strip kit I bought from the garden shop. The reading looked like pH 7.5, and the nitrite square was close to zero. The nitrate color was between ten and twenty, so I wrote down fifteen as an estimate, not an exact reading. The water was about sixty-eight degrees in the afternoon. The kit's chart is printed in tiny colors, and I may have read the nitrate a shade too high. I want to repeat it in the morning with daylight on the chart. I did not add any treatment because the fish are acting normally, and I don't want to change two things at once. One of the goldfish came up for food and then went back under the lily leaves. The other two stayed near the stones.

There are three pots in the pond. One has a dwarf water lily, and two have rushes. The lily sent up a new leaf, but the older leaf has a brown edge. I pinched off the soft part and left the firm green part alone. I added a little gravel around the top of the pot because the fish keep nosing into the soil. The rush in the back left pot is leaning toward the light, and I turned the pot a quarter turn, not all the way around, because I don't want to disturb the roots. The floating basket has a few duckweed leaves in it now. I skimmed out most of the loose duckweed, but left a small patch in the corner for shade. I should check that patch again after the next windy day.

Here is the list of things I want to do before the next rain:
1. Clear the maple leaves from the mesh cover and check whether its corner clips are still holding.
2. Rinse the filter sponge in water taken from the pond and keep the replacement sponge dry on the shelf.
3. Take another water reading in daylight and write the date beside it.
4. Look for the screwdriver and read the pump instructions again before opening anything.
5. Trim the dead lily edge only if it has turned fully brown.

I haven't ordered more plants, and I'm not sure the shelf has room for another pot, so I should measure it before I go back to the nursery.

I talked with Mara over the fence while she was watering her tomatoes. She said, “My small pond gets cloudy whenever I move the gravel.” I told her mine did that last spring for a few hours after I moved a pot, but it cleared by the next morning. We didn't compare water tests, and I don't know what kind of filter she uses. She offered me a handful of water mint cuttings, and I said I would think about it because it spreads quickly if the pot tips over. I don't want to put it loose in the pond. I may ask her where she keeps hers contained when I see her again.

The stone path beside the pond is still damp in the morning, and one of the flat stones rocks slightly when I step on its outer edge. I put a small orange marker beside it so I remember not to carry the full watering can across that spot. The marker is not a repair, and I should reset the stone before anyone trips. I have a spare bag of coarse sand in the shed, but I need to check that it has not clumped from last winter. The shed key is on the hook by the back door, and the sand is behind the empty clay pots. I could do the stone on the same trip as the pump check if the ground is dry.

For now, the pond looks calm, and the fish are eating, but I will keep an eye on the water level because the warm spell has lasted longer than I expected. The mark on the flat rock is about an inch below the waterline from last week, and that could be evaporation. I haven't topped it up yet. The garden hose was left in the sun yesterday, so I will run it briefly away from the pond before using it. I would rather add a little water slowly than fill the pond in one go and stir up the bottom. I should also put the test strips back in their sealed pouch. The box sat open on the bench while I was writing the readings. That's all for this memo."}]
